title: Who ran it, who bought it, who buried it
lede: Roles and dates are from the filings and press cited. The founders of Soft Warehouse are not named in the sources we could open, so they are not named here.

people.name: Nathan Morton
people.role: President and CEO from late 1989; chairman in 1993
people.text: A former Home Depot executive with no background in computers, hired to roll out the superstores. Sales rose from $66M in fiscal 1988 to $600M in 1990. He resigned at a board meeting in December 1993.[^8]

people.name: Ronald N. Dubin
people.role: Led the 1989 investor group; chairman until 1993
people.text: His group acquired Soft Warehouse in January 1989.[^8]

people.name: James F. Halpin
people.text: Came from the Home Base home-improvement chain six months before taking over, and was still president and chief executive when the sale to Grupo Sanborns was announced in January 2000. A Dallas jury returned a $175.5M verdict against him personally in 2001, which the trial judge set aside.[^8][^1][^5][^9]
people.later: Described as CompUSA’s former chief executive in a filing covering 2001.[^9]

people.name: Carlos Slim Domit
people.text: Announced the purchase in January 2000 and said the buyers could “re-energize the organization.”[^5]

people.name: Carlos Slim Helú
people.text: The AP described CompUSA in 2007 as controlled by his Grupo Carso. Computerworld, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported that he had put about $2 billion into the chain since 1999.[^13][^14]

people.name: Roman Ross
people.text: Announced the closing of 126 stores in February 2007 and moved to an advisory role when Gordon Brothers took over in December.[^11][^13]

people.name: Bill Weinstein and Stephen Gray
people.text: A Gordon Brothers principal and the managing partner of CRG Partners. eWeek reported them as interim president and chief restructuring officer.[^13][^15]

people.name: Richard Leeds and Gilbert Fiorentino
people.text: Bought the name, the website and 16 stores. Leeds retired the brand in 2012.[^16][^19]
